newsitem.title: UK: Britain warns China on Hong Kong legislature plan.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns China on Hong Kong legislature plan.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind on Thursday warned China it risked creating "confusion and uncertainty" in Hong Kong if it rushed ahead with plans to set up its own provisional legislature for the territory.

Rifkind said the move would raise the question of whether Beijing really intended to abide by its "joint declaration" agreement with Britain for the handover of the colony's sovereignty in June next year.

"Its establishment and operation of a parallel legislature before the handover would seriously call into question China's commitment to its obligations under the joint declaration," Rifkind told the British parliament.
China has recently appointed a 400-person body to select a new legislature for Hong Kong to replace the colonial legislative council.
Rifkind said it seemed determined to set up such a body as early as next month, to run in parallel with the Legislative Council until next June.

If it did so, said Rifkind, "China would have to explain to Hong Kong and the world why they have chosen to replace a body for which more than a million Hong Kong people voted by one chosen by a handpicked electorate of only 400".
"We continue to make clear to the Chinese, in public and in private at every level, that their planned provisional legislature is neither desirable nor necessary," he added.

Rifkind said the row over the legislature, plus China's failure to state how it will carry out promises on human rights when it assumes sovereignty, were marring success in reaching agreement on other issues relating to next year's handover.
He said Hong Kong economically was performing well as it moved towards the handover, defying prophets who had predicted it would go into decline ahead of 1997.
"Hong Kong is not just lasting the course; it is entering the final lap of its transition in top form," he said.

Earlier in Hong Kong, legislative council member Martin Lee said he had appealed to ministers to make clear during the parliamentary debate which Rifkind was opening that the setting up of the new legislature would breach the joint declaration.
"I'm afraid the indications are they would not say it," Lee, the leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, said on his return from a visit to London.
